(BTW, homeopathy also has preventative claims, but again, with no better proof than the alleged cures.)

The reason why homeopathy is considered quack medicine and vaccination isn't is not because of where it applies: it's because homeopathy has no scientific basis (the claims about why it should work have never withstood testing, so there is currentlys no known way by which it could work better than placebo), and because, in fact, it has not been shown to work better than placebo. Those are literally the only important thing.

To promote homeopathy to the rank of actual medicine it needs to show that it at the very least works better than placebo. And ideally, it should also be possible to get a general idea about the why. (The latter isn't necessary, but it helps against skpetics.)

Overall, if a person is willing to put the homeopathic item under FDA approval structure and let it fly, I'm OK with it, even if it is inert. The placebo effect is real, so if someone can cure themselves by taking some snake oil, who am I to tell them no?

That's a different issue though. As long as it doesn't make claims about being effective …
